summary: Defines the MESSAGE method, an extension to the Session Initiation Protocol that lets instant messages be sent between users in near real time. The messages are usually short and used conversationally. It gives SIP a basic way to carry text chat without setting up a session.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3428 adds MESSAGE, a SIP method for sending a message that stands on its own. The request can pass through SIP proxies without setting up a conversation session.

how does sip instant messaging work

subtitle: A SIP method for sending stand-alone instant messages through SIP routing.

tldr.problem: SIP supported presence and session-based communication but did not define a method for sending stand-alone instant messages.
tldr.mechanism: The MESSAGE method carries an instant message in a MIME body and follows normal SIP routing. A MESSAGE request does not create a dialog.
tldr.outcome: SIP gained a pager-style message exchange with size, congestion and security requirements. RFC 3428 is updated by RFC 8591.

facts.label: Maximum size outside a media session

today: RFC 3428 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2002. It has been updated by RFC 8591.

sections.title: The Pager Model of Instant Messaging
sections.content:
Instant messaging is the near-real-time exchange of content between participants. Messages are often short and may form a conversation in the user interface. RFC 3428 adds the SIP MESSAGE method to carry that content in a request body.

The RFC covers the pager model: each message stands alone, with no explicit association between successive messages. It does not define the session model, which has a beginning and end. Implementations SHOULD NOT create SIP dialogs mainly to associate MESSAGE requests with one another.
sections.plainLanguage: MESSAGE sends one item of content without creating a continuing session. A user interface may group several messages into a conversation, but the protocol does not do so.

sections.title: How a MESSAGE Request Travels
sections.content:
The sender creates a SIP request whose method is MESSAGE. Its body contains the content, and the body may use any MIME type. The Request-URI normally names the recipient's address of record, though it may name a device when the sender knows the recipient's location.

SIP proxies route the request using normal SIP rules and may fork it to multiple terminals. A 200 OK from the final user agent means that agent accepted the message; it does not prove the user read it. A MESSAGE request does not establish a dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The MESSAGE request carries the content through the SIP network to a receiving user agent. A success response confirms acceptance by that agent, not that a person has read the message.

sections.title: Sender, Receiver and Response Rules
sections.content:
A sending user agent MUST be prepared to send text/plain and MUST NOT put a Contact header in a MESSAGE request. The receiving user agent MUST be prepared to receive and render plain text. It SHOULD return a final response immediately, but is not required to display the message.

A relay or store-and-forward service SHOULD return 202 Accepted; this confirms that it accepted the message but does not guarantee final delivery. A 2xx response MUST have no body. The method name is case-sensitive, and an Instant Message URI has the form im:user@domain; clients SHOULD resolve it to a SIP URI before sending.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver answers promptly, but a reply code does not say whether a user saw the message. A relay's 202 response means it accepted the message for possible later delivery.

sections.title: Message Size and Congestion
sections.content:
MESSAGE carries the communication itself, unlike SIP requests that usually set up or modify a media session. High message traffic could interfere with call signaling. MESSAGE requests SHOULD use a transport with end-to-end congestion control, such as TCP or SCTP.

Outside a media session, a MESSAGE request MUST NOT exceed 1300 bytes unless the sender knows that it will not cross a congestion-unsafe link or that it is at least 200 bytes below the lowest path MTU. A sender MUST NOT start a second out-of-dialog MESSAGE transaction to the same URI while the first is pending.
sections.plainLanguage: Large messages can contribute to network congestion. The RFC limits their size outside a media session and prevents overlapping requests to the same destination.

sections.title: A Message Through a Proxy
sections.content:
The RFC's example has User 1 send a MESSAGE with a text/plain body to User 2 through a proxy. The proxy looks up the recipient's registered device address and forwards the request there.

User 2's agent returns 200 OK. The proxy sends that response back along the Via path. The example illustrates that the request and response use ordinary SIP routing for a non-INVITE method.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, a proxy finds the recipient's registered device, forwards the text, and returns the device's response to the sender.

sections.title: Protecting Message Content
sections.content:
Because MESSAGE carries the actual communication, user agents that support it MUST implement end-to-end authentication, body integrity and body confidentiality mechanisms. The RFC specifies S/MIME support, including encryption with CMS EnvelopedData and signatures with CMS SignedData.

Hop-by-hop secure connections do not hide unencrypted bodies from proxies. Signed requests and responses MUST include a Date header covered by the signature to help prevent replay. A stale date can also occur in legitimate store-and-forward delivery, so receivers need to account for that case.
sections.plainLanguage: A MESSAGE body needs protection from reading and changes while it travels. A signed date helps detect old messages that an attacker tries to replay.
